interactive.title: Finish the square
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on completing the square. On the left, x² + bx is drawn as tiles, as in lesson 1: an x by x square, and beside it a strip b wide and x long. You cut the strip in half and drag one half round to the bottom of the square, so both sides of the square grow by the same amount and the pieces nearly make a bigger square with sides x + b ÷ 2. One corner is left empty, b ÷ 2 by b ÷ 2, and it flashes: that is the number you add to finish the square and take off again so the value does not change. A slider sets b from 0 to 10 in steps of 2, so the corner reads 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 or 25. On the right is the parabola y = x² + bx + c, a sketch drawn from its rule, with its lowest point marked; as b grows the point slides to x = −b ÷ 2, where the square is zero, and drops to c − (b ÷ 2)², the plain number less the corner. Screens: 1 cuts x² + 6x into a square of side x + 3 with a 3 by 3 corner missing; 2 asks for the corner of x² + 8x; 3 gives the b slider and the rule, checked at x = 1; 4 asks which form is x² + 10x; 5 adds the 2 of x² + 6x + 2 as two small squares in the corner, leaving 7 empty; 6 asks for x² + 4x + 1; 7 shows the lowest point (−3, −7) and the line of symmetry x = −3, with the slider; 8 asks for the turning point of (x − 4)² + 3; 9 solves x² + 6x + 2 = 0; 10 asks for the next line of x² + 4x + 1 = 0; 11 shows −x² + 4x + 10 as an upside-down U, highest at (2, 14); 12 to 14 mix it all, the last with a minus in front of x². From screen 8 the signs include minus, which an area cannot show, so the tiles step aside and the working lines and the graph carry it. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to pick one answer from three. A wrong pick puts a number into both forms, or its point into the rule, and shows they disagree.
interactive.ignores: The square's side x is drawn at one fixed length, but the two forms agree for every x, negative or a fraction included; a tile just cannot have a negative side, which is why minus signs are shown by working and the graph instead. b moves in steps of 2 only to keep half of it whole; any b works, so x² + 5x is (x + 2.5)² − 6.25. The parabola is drawn only over the stretch of x on screen; it carries on rising either side.

explain.text:
Completing the square rewrites a quadratic as a perfect square plus a number.[^1] x² + 6x + 2 becomes (x + 3)² − 7, and that form tells you at once its lowest value, −7, and where it happens, at x = −3.

Here is where the square comes from. On the picture, x² + 6x is an x by x square with a strip 6 wide beside it. A square needs both its sides lengthened by the same amount, so the strip is shared equally: cut it into two strips 3 wide and move one round to the bottom. The pieces now nearly fill a square with sides x + 3. Only a 3 by 3 corner is missing, because (x + 3)² is x² + 6x + 9, the perfect square from lesson 2. So x² + 6x is that square less its corner: x² + 6x = (x + 3)² − 9. Adding the corner and taking it off again changes nothing, which a number confirms: at x = 1, 1 + 6 = 7 and 16 − 9 = 7. Leave the corner on and (x + 3)² gives 16 there, not 7. The 2 on the end just comes along: x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7. Whatever the number in front of x, half of it goes on each side, so the corner is (b ÷ 2)², and x² + bx + c = (x + b ÷ 2)² + c − (b ÷ 2)². This is MathWorld's general rule for the case where x² has no number in front.[^2] The move is called [[completing the square]], and (x + 3)² − 7 is the quadratic's [[completed-square form]]. It also finishes the x² + 4x + 1 that lesson 2 could not factorise: x² + 4x + 1 = (x + 2)² − 4 + 1 = (x + 2)² − 3.

The square is what shows the lowest value. The square of any number on the number line is never below zero, and (x + 3)² is zero only when x + 3 = 0, at x = −3. So (x + 3)² − 7 is never below −7, and it is −7 exactly at x = −3. On the graph that is the turning point from Calculus fundamentals, (−3, −7), the bottom of the U (some books call it the vertex); the completed-square form gives its coordinates.[^3] Calculus agrees: the slope of x² + 6x + 2 is 2x + 6, which is zero at x = −3. Points the same distance either side of −3 give the same square, so x = −1 and x = −5 both give 4 − 7 = −3, and the curve is a mirror image about the upright line x = −3, its [[line of symmetry]].[^3] Drag the slider and the same reasoning moves the point: (x + b ÷ 2)² is zero at x = −b ÷ 2, so the lowest point sits there, and its height is c less the corner, so it drops by exactly the corner as b grows. A minus inside the bracket puts the turning point on the plus side: x − 4 is zero at x = 4, so (x − 4)² + 3 turns at (4, 3), just as f(x − 4) slides 4 right in Functions and their graphs. In the same way, the whole graph of x² + 6x + 2 is y = x² slid 3 left and 7 down.

The halving works on a single x², so a number in front is taken out of the x² and x terms first. With a minus in front: −x² + 4x + 10 = −(x² − 4x) + 10, and x² − 4x = (x − 2)² − 4, so it is −((x − 2)² − 4) + 10 = −(x − 2)² + 4 + 10 = −(x − 2)² + 14. Now the square is taken away, so the turning point is a highest value, 14 at x = 2, on an upside-down U. With a 2 in front: 2x² + 12x + 5 = 2(x² + 6x) + 5 = 2((x + 3)² − 9) + 5, and the corner comes off twice, 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 5 = 2(x + 3)² − 13. Its most common use is solving quadratic equations.[^1] x² + 6x + 2 = 0 has no whole-number pair, but take the 2 across, x² + 6x = −2, and add the corner 9 to both sides, so it stays balanced: (x + 3)² = 7. A number squared makes 7 when it is √7 or −√7, so x + 3 = ±√7 and x = −3 ± √7, about −0.35 or −5.65. Both sit 2.65 from the line of symmetry, one each side.

One plain note on your aim: the MCA's Second Engineer maths list asks you to state and use the general formula for a quadratic,[^4] and SQA's Engineering Mathematics 1 asks for good algebraic skills on entry,[^5] but none of the lines read for this course names completing the square. It is taught anyway because it is what makes the formula in lesson 5, and the turning point on the graph, make sense.

**Halve the number in front of x, add its square to finish a perfect square and take it off again: x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7, so its lowest value is −7, at x = −3.[^3]**

analogy.text: Think of an electricity bill made of a standing charge plus a charge for the units you use. The units part can never go below zero, so the lowest the bill can ever be is the standing charge, in a month when you use nothing. The completed-square form is built the same way: (x + 3)² is the part that can never go below zero, −7 is the fixed part, so the lowest value is −7, reached where the square is zero, at x = −3.
analogy.breaks: The units charge only rises one way, as you use more, while (x + 3)² rises on both sides of x = −3, and faster the further out you go. And a standing charge is never negative, while the fixed number in a completed-square form, like this −7, can be.

practice.text:
- If there is a number in front of x², take it out of the x² and x terms first, because the halving finishes a square from a single x².
- Halve the number in front of x and write (x + half)², keeping its sign.
- Take off half squared, because that corner was not in the rule; with a number taken out, it comes off that many times.
- Bring along the plain number on the end.
- Check by putting x = 0 into both forms: they must give the same.
- Read it: (x + p)² + q has its turning point at x = −p, height q, and its line of symmetry is x = −p.
- To solve (x + p)² + q = 0, take q across and square-root both sides, with ±.

**Rule of thumb:** The turning point's x is the number that makes the bracket zero, so the sign flips; the number outside is its height as it stands. A plus in front of x² gives a lowest value, a minus a highest.

**Worked example:** In Calculus fundamentals you found the bottom of 2x² − 12x + 25 at x = 3, where its slope 4x − 12 is zero. Completing the square finds it without the slope. Take the 2 out: 2(x² − 6x) + 25. Half of −6 is −3, so x² − 6x = (x − 3)² − 9. Then 2((x − 3)² − 9) + 25 = 2(x − 3)² − 18 + 25 = 2(x − 3)² + 7. Check at x = 0: 2 × 9 + 7 = 25, as the rule gives. A square is never below zero, so the lowest value is 7, at x = 3, the same answer as the slope gave.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting to take the corner off, so x² + 10x becomes (x + 5)². At x = 1 that is 36, not 11.
- Adding the corner to one side only when solving, so x² + 4x = −1 becomes (x + 2)² = −1. Add 4 to both sides: (x + 2)² = 3.
- Reading the turning point with the bracket's sign, so (x − 4)² + 3 turns at x = −4. There the rule gives 67, not 3.
- Halving before taking out the number in front, so 2x² + 12x + 5 becomes 2(x + 6)² − 13. At x = 0 that is 59, not 5. Take out the 2 first: 2(x + 3)² − 13.
- Taking one square root, so (x + 3)² = 7 gives only x = −3 + √7. −3 − √7 works too.
